    Structs: grouping related data

    By the end, you will be able to

    • Define and construct a named-field Task struct.
    • Read and update fields while respecting ownership.
    • Use field shorthand and Debug printing.
    • Recognize when struct update syntax, tuple structs, and unit-like structs fit.

    Prerequisite: Module 2: Ownership and borrowing. This lesson starts the Task example used throughout Module 3.

    A task is one value with related fields

    A task needs an identifier and a title. Passing these as unrelated values makes it easy to mix up which title belongs to which ID. A struct gives the pair one name while keeping each field's type clear.

    struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
}

let task = Task {
    id: 1,
    title: String::from("Read the Rust book"),
};
println!("{}: {}", task.id, task.title);

    The field names are part of the type. Construction must provide both fields with the declared types. Task owns its String title. A binding must be mutable to replace a field:

    let mut task = Task {
    id: 1,
    title: String::from("Read the Rust book"),
};
task.title = String::from("Practice structs");

    Checkpoint 1

    Which value can construct this Task?




    Field shorthand and ownership

    When a variable has the same name as a field, write the name once. This moves the String into the struct, just as writing title: title would.

    let title = String::from("Read the Rust book");
let task = Task { id: 1, title };
// println!("{title}"); // Error: title was moved into task.

    Ownership reminder

    String::from("Read the Rust book") creates an owned String. Assigning that value to title gives the binding ownership, and using title in Task { id: 1, title } moves that ownership into the struct. The original title binding cannot be used afterward unless you borrow or clone the string first.

    Reading task.title for display borrows it for the print call. An explicit borrow can be useful when passing the field to an API that accepts &str:

    println!("{}", task.title.as_str());
println!("{}", task.id); // task is still usable.

    Moving the owned field into another variable is different. After a partial move, Rust still allows access to the untouched Copy field id, but the whole Task can no longer be used as a value.

    let title = task.title;
println!("{title}");
println!("{}", task.id);
// println!("{}", task.title); // Error: title was moved out.

    Checkpoint 2

    After let task = Task { id: 1, title };, what happens to the original title: String binding?




    Inspect the value with Debug

    Add #[derive(Debug)] above the definition to print all fields while learning or diagnosing a program. {:?} uses that derived formatting behavior. Module 4 explains the trait behind it.

    #[derive(Debug)]
struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
}

let task = Task { id: 1, title: String::from("Read") };
println!("{task:?}"); // Task { id: 1, title: "Read" }

    Checkpoint 3

    What enables println!("{task:?}") for this struct?




    Complete runnable example

    This file combines construction, shorthand, mutation, borrowing, debug printing, and a partial move:

    #[derive(Debug)]
struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
}

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Read the Rust book");
    let mut task = Task { id: 1, title };

    println!("task: {task:?}");
    println!("title: {}", task.title.as_str());

    task.title = String::from("Practice structs");
    println!("updated: {task:?}");

    let title = task.title;
    println!("moved title: {title}");
    println!("remaining id: {}", task.id);
}

    From the repository root, with the stable Rust toolchain installed:

    rustc examples/03-structs-enums-and-data-modeling/01-structs/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-task-structs
/tmp/rust-task-structs

    Expected output:

    task: Task { id: 1, title: "Read the Rust book" }
title: Read the Rust book
updated: Task { id: 1, title: "Practice structs" }
moved title: Practice structs
remaining id: 1

    The demo's README in examples/03-structs-enums-and-data-modeling/01-structs/ records its prerequisites and limitations.

    Small extensions

    Struct update syntax copies or moves fields from an existing value. Here the new title is supplied and id, a Copy value, comes from first:

    let first = Task { id: 1, title: String::from("Read") };
let second = Task { title: String::from("Practice"), ..first };
println!("{} {}", first.id, second.title);

    Checkpoint 4

    After the struct update above, which field comes from first?




    A tuple struct gives a value its own type without naming its fields. In TaskId(u32), the parentheses declare one field of type u32. Construct it with TaskId(1) and read its first field with .0: the zero is the field's position, while 1 is the task ID stored there. A tuple struct with two fields would use .0 and .1. Use named fields for Task, where id and title have different meanings.

    struct TaskId(u32);

let id = TaskId(1);
println!("task ID: {}", id.0); // task ID: 1

    A unit-like struct has no fields or stored values. For example, struct Marker; declares a type whose value can be written as Marker.

    Exercise

    1. Add a priority: u8 field to Task and update every construction site.
    2. Print the priority, then change it through a mutable Task binding.
    3. Change the title through the same binding and check the full value with Debug.
    4. Comment out let title = task.title; in the demo and compare which later uses of task become possible. Restore it afterward.

    Expected result: the program compiles, prints the new priority, and still shows the updated title. A construction missing priority should produce a compiler diagnostic that points to the missing field.

    Final checkpoint

    Why is a named-field struct a good starting model for a task?
